MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: Divine command and human nature directly touch religious moral reasoning. Other major parts develop philosophical ethics and normative argument with no established comparative study of religious ethics.

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.contribution: Craft and material production are explicitly related to religious, social and gendered identities across ancient societies. This is substantive relevant material, while the course remains organised around archaeology and making rather than comparison of religious practices.
MCCHEAM112.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.contribution: Social influence on thoughts/feelings/behaviour is relevant to belief in a broad sense. The source does not establish religious belief, religious experience or religious coping; the earlier interest ownership silently broadened religious belief to belief generally.
HCBPSYC111.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.contribution: Organised religion is explicitly one of several themes in a broad literary survey. This supports a bounded contribution, without turning the whole course into scripture, Christian history or comparative religion.

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.contribution: Cross-cultural myth, literary transmission, oral/visual forms and comparison are directly relevant. Retain the partial VU myth correspondence; VU also teaches ritual and the disciplinary debate in myth/ritual studies, so equivalence is not claimed.
MCCLITR211.topics: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.contribution: Aquinas, natural law and rights in traditional societies are concrete relevant content. Their role within a broad rights course does not supply sustained study of religious claims or communities.
GOSLAWJ111.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy

GOSSOCI214.name: Modern Sociology
GOSSOCI214.contribution: Modernity, imperialism and colonial responses can contextualise religious change. The supplied profile does not establish an inquiry into religious change; that application cannot simply be assumed.
GOSSOCI214.topics: Modernity and Eurocentrism; Functionalism; Frankfurt School critical theory; Black feminist thought and intersectionality; Social construction of reality; Symbolic interactionism; Stigma and othering; Social space, capital and art; Coloniality and postcolonialism; Decolonial and Indigenous sociology; Gender and power

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology

MCCHEAM315.contribution: The profile explicitly connects Athenian democracy, myth and religion through material heritage and simulation. It is a strong concrete case contribution, but its organising subject is ancient democracy rather than sustained comparative religious inquiry.

MCCLITR312.contribution: Humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural-minority and psychoanalytic readings plus a text project supply real methods. The evidence does not establish sacred-text interpretation or dialogue across religious traditions. A possible religious text choice is not a required programme component.
MCCLITR312.topics: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.contribution: The description includes Islamic courts within Renaissance artistic exchange. It documents an artistic context, not Islamic belief, religious interpretation or spiritual practice. No enriched profile is available; only documented description scope is used.
MCCHEAM212.topics: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.contribution: description2 includes religious constitutions; the profile covers comparative constitutional/administrative law. This supports a limited religion/state perspective, not comparative religious traditions or the interpretation of their beliefs. GOSLAWJ213.topics: Constitutional origins and fundamental features; Federalism and decentralization; Parliaments and lawmaking; Governments and heads of state; Court systems and judicial review; Constitutional rights; EU constitutional order; Administrative-law functions; Public participation; Administrative remedies; Procedural fairness, discretion and legitimate expectations

distinctness.reason: The second plan is a targeted three-course refinement of the first. It is not proposed as a distinct option.

coverageSearch.judgment: Screened all active titles and evidence and read the nearby humanities and social science offerings. Additional visual art, spiritual travel writing and Indigenous history were tested. Greek Archaeology concerns community and democracy; Writing Art’s Histories supplies interpretation; media courses address representation; general environmental and clinical courses do not establish a religion-focused environmental or mental health strand.

findings.concept: Comparative religious cultures, texts and worldviews
findings.assessment: The strongest feasible interdisciplinary plan includes direct work on myth and partial work on philosophy, belief, religious material culture and spiritual self-representation. Its complementary research and interpretive methods do not supply sustained work across religious traditions, sacred texts or lived practice.

Actual conflict, radicalisation and environmental courses can supply complementary perspectives; no required religion-centred inquiry or documented religious-environment/dialogue sequence is established. Rejection as merely redundant with the withdrawn public-life strand is superseded.

The specific art/literary/philosophical contributions do not establish theological/biblical interpretation, doctrine or lived-faith formation. Missing professional credentials are not used to reject the general comparative route.

Islamic courts as artistic context and comparative public law do not establish Islamic belief, history, exegesis or jurisprudence. Arabic remains support-only under the retained corrected evidence classification.

alignment: World Myth & Literature supports a partial myth-and-ritual relationship through cross-cultural myth, but VU separately examines ritual and its disciplinary study. Western Philosophy partly supports World Philosophy; freedom of religion and religious constitutions add public-life material without supplying Islamic jurisprudence. Ethics and Buddhist non-self are genuine specific contributions. Research methodology and literary reading are transferable; the required religion-specific application, sacred-text interpretation and cumulative comparative study remain absent. No public UCR schedule or course modal is selected.
